Right? When I reload, I use the cheapest combination of powder, primers, and bullets/shot I can. Why use new lead shot when I can buy reclaimed for far cheaper. Why use 1 oz when 7/8 breaks clays just fine. I'm not looking for pinpoint accuracy from my 9mm, so the cheapest FMJ bullets will work great.

If you care about your barrel though, don't buy steel cased ammo.

While the carbine firing Federal ammunition maintained acceptable accuracy up to and including the 10,000 round mark, the Brown Bear and Wolf carbines exhibited significant accuracy loss by the 6,000 round mark. It is quite possible that this first started occurring earlier than 6,000 rounds, because groups at 4,000 were well within standards of 5MOA or less, while some shots at 6,000 “keyholed,” or impacted the target sideways.

Basically, steel cased ammo uses bi-metal coating instead of copper jackets. The bi-metal coating (aka steel and copper) will wear your barrel at least 2-3 times as fast.
So, does that mean Hornady HP is out?

Why? As far as I know, Hornady only uses copper jackets. I'd be surprised if a high end US company like Hornady uses cheaper steel bimetal jackets.

Also, the ammo tested was cheap Russian bullets.
I stand corrected. After embarrassingly easy research, it turns out they use nickel plated copper. I will keep using Hornady with impunity, then. Carry on.

the important points are thus: steal is cheaper but not suitable for reloading. copper is more expensive but can be reloaded and won't wear/damage the barrel. also "cheap" ammo (typcally steel) can sometimes use highly corrosive primer which causes further wear and damage. for example this is often the case for the boxes of old military surplus ammo. so it may be less expensive up front but you still pay for it one way or another.
